Abstract and introduction state the frontier result broadly before fully foregrounding the fixed-threshold and triangular-array gates; revise the first contribution paragraph to state the result as applying for fixed t0>0 under the listed overlap, envelope, second-moment, degrading-array, and sampling-ratio conditions.

The receipt-transport discussion gives a validation template but leaves the substantive strength of the average denominator restriction underdeveloped; add a short paragraph after \cref{obj:ass:receipt-transport} explaining what target-side evidence makes the average equality credible and how it differs from conditional receipt transport.

The literature discussion is accurate but often catalog-like; sharpen the comparison to ChenHuang2025, RudolphVanderLaan2017, Ma2023, and SmuclerLanniMasip2025 by stating the exact object each studies and the exact added frontier or transport-dispersion result here.

The main text repeats long assumption checklists inside definitions and theorem statements, which slows the paper's argument; move repeated inherited lists to a compact table or a single model-summary paragraph and keep theorem statements focused on incremental conditions.

The proof appendix reads partly as a verification transcript, with mechanical steps such as inhabitedness and empty-row handling interrupting the econometric argument; create a short proof-sketch layer in the appendix and relegate Lean bookkeeping details to the verification note.

The feasible finite-cell procedures are described as implementation benchmarks, but the data requirements are easy to miss; add a concise paragraph before \cref{obj:thm:finite-cell-unknown-weight-attainment} listing the observed inputs, known design quantities, and growth conditions needed for the sample-only claim.

The abstract and introduction state the two-sided characterization \(V^\star(t_0)\asymp\min\{1,t_0^{-1/2}\}\) as if the lower bound were established over the full transported class \(\mathcal P_n\), but the proof of \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} derives it from a single unit-weight geometry (\(w\equiv1\), \(e\equiv1/2\), uniform \(k_n\) cells) via \cref{obj:prop:no-shift-reduction}. The lower bound is thus driven entirely by first-stage weakness on a slice where \(\kappa_n=1\), and the constants \(c_0,t_c\) do not depend on \(\kappa_n\) at all; the abstract's sentence 'The unit-transport-weight least-favorable slice is embedded in the transported class, so its weak-ratio lower bound applies to the larger transported model' is accurate but is then followed by 'Up to constants... the same order holds conditionally on any admissible fixed covariate-shift geometry,' which invites the reading that dispersion is shown to be necessary. Fix: in the abstract and in the paragraph after \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse}, state explicitly that the converse is witnessed on a no-shift slice and that the role of \(\kappa_n\) in the lower bound enters through \cref{obj:thm:fixed-geometry-frontier}, whose least-favorable family calibrates \(\mu_n=(t_0\kappa_n/n)^{1/2}\) at each admissible geometry.

\Cref{obj:ass:receipt-transport} (receipt-contrast transport) is imposed only as an equality of \(P_T\)-averages, not conditionally in \(x\), while \cref{obj:ass:outcome-transport} is conditional. The text flags the asymmetry in one sentence ('this distinction is the transport structure used by the identification result below') and the post-assumption gloss says it 'allow[s] covariate-specific receipt contrasts to differ,' but the paper never discusses what this buys or costs: an averaged condition is weaker and hence attractive, yet it is also not implied by the usual conditional-exchangeability-of-sampling justifications that would motivate \cref{obj:ass:outcome-transport}, and it can hold by cancellation across \(x\) in ways a reader would not endorse substantively. Fix: add a short paragraph after \cref{obj:ass:receipt-transport} giving (i) a primitive sufficient condition (e.g. conditional receipt transport plus \cref{obj:ass:transport-domination}) that implies it, and (ii) one concrete example where the averaged version holds while the conditional version fails, so the reader can judge whether the weakening is substantive or an artifact of what the identification proof needs.

The assumptions are each followed by a single sentence, nearly all of the template form 'X is the standard ... condition ... \\citep{ChenHuang2025}', with eleven consecutive glosses citing the same paper. This is uninformative in two ways: it does not say which conditions are genuinely inherited from the cited transported-CACE design and which are new here, and it substitutes an appeal to standardness for a discussion of restrictiveness. The three conditions doing the most work — \cref{obj:ass:weight-envelope} (\(w\le 2k_n\)), \cref{obj:ass:weight-second-moment} (\(\kappa_n\le k_n\)), and \cref{obj:ass:degrading-array} (\(k_n\to\infty\), \(k_n=o(\sqrt n)\), \(\mu_n\to0\)) — are labelled 'specific to this analysis' but never interrogated. Fix: replace the repeated boilerplate with one consolidated paragraph attributing the inherited IV/transport block to \citet{ChenHuang2025} and \citet{ImbensAngrist1994}, and add a dedicated subsection discussing (a) why the envelope must diverge rather than stay bounded, (b) what design features make \(\kappa_n\le k_n\) binding versus slack, and (c) what fails when \(k_n\asymp\sqrt n\) or faster, since \(k_n=o(\sqrt n)\) is exactly the gate the feasible cell-learning results lean on.

The feasible results are consistently described as removing the oracle, but the two constructions retain substantial known structure that the surrounding prose underweights. \Cref{obj:thm:finite-cell-unknown-weight-attainment} requires known equal source cell masses \(1/k_n\), known propensity \(1/2\), and a known cell partition; \cref{obj:thm:regular-cell-unknown-weight-attainment} requires known \(q_{x,n}\) and known \(e_{x,n}\). Only the target cell frequencies are learned. Yet the section is titled 'Feasible Cell Weight Learning', the introduction says these procedures 'replace oracle-known weights by target-sample learning', and the abstract says they 'learn the target weights from the target covariate sample' — all true, but a reader will infer more nuisance-estimation content than is delivered. Fix: in the introduction paragraph and at the head of the finite-cell subsection, state the input list affirmatively in one sentence ('the procedures take the cell partition, source cell masses, and propensities as known and estimate only the target cell frequencies and the collision scale'), and rename the section to reflect target-frequency learning specifically.

Positioning against the two closest antecedents is asserted rather than demonstrated. The 'Transported noncompliance' and 'Weak-IV and two-sample IV inference' paragraphs each end with a one-line 'The present paper adds ...' claim, but the paper never states what \citet{ChenHuang2025} assume about first-stage strength (regular versus degrading), nor what \citet{Ma2023} and \citet{SmuclerLanniMasip2025} deliver in the way of length guarantees, so the reader cannot verify that the expected-length frontier is genuinely new rather than a reindexing of known weak-IV length results through \(\kappa_n\). Fix: expand each paragraph with two sentences giving the antecedent's regime and guarantee explicitly (e.g. 'ChenHuang2025 establish \(\sqrt n\)-consistency and asymptotic normality under a fixed positive target complier share; the present arrays allow \(\mu_n\to0\)'), so the delta is checkable against the cited statements.

The appendix's treatment of the presentation-synthesized objects understates a structural oddity that a reader will notice: \cref{obj:def:geometry-handle} is stated as a definition ('Geometry handle') but its content is a pair of inequalities — the chi-square bound \(1+\chi^2\le\exp(8t_0h^2)\) and \(\|Q_{n,h}^{\mathfrak g}-Q_{n,0}^{\mathfrak g}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le2\rho\) — that are load-bearing lemmas in the proof of \cref{obj:thm:fixed-geometry-frontier} (Step 1 cites it for the TV bound). It also duplicates the parameter definitions \(\mu_n,p_n,\rho\) already given in \cref{obj:def:least-favorable-witness}, and both carry the same displayed symbol \(Q_{n,h}^{\mathfrak g}\). Fix: merge the parameter block into \cref{obj:def:least-favorable-witness}, restate the two bounds as a lemma with its own verification status in the appendix table, and drop the redundant 'handle' environment so the reader can see which closeness bounds are checked and which are expository.

Introduction and abstract: the claim that the frontier holds over the transported model should foreground the oracle inputs and triangular-array gates each time the headline rate is stated; revise the first rate paragraph to read as an oracle expected-length frontier under fixed overlap, bounded outcomes, envelope, second-moment, degrading-array, and effective-strength restrictions.

Setup, transport assumptions: several assumptions are described as "standard," especially receipt-contrast transport and outcome-contrast transport, although their exact mix is tailored to this paper; replace broad standardness language with a short explanation of the population equality each condition imposes and why it identifies the transported numerator or denominator.

Oracle score attainment theorem: the "Admissible geometry" bullet feels like an ambient nonemptiness device rather than a statistical condition for the procedure; move that explanatory sentence into the theorem statement or a remark immediately after it so readers understand why a fixed geometry appears in an oracle theorem over \mathcal P_n.

Finite-cell section: the implementation paragraph blends recipe, theorem interpretation, and benchmark status; split it into a short constructive paragraph before the theorem and a post-theorem interpretation paragraph stating the exact known inputs, learned quantities, and growth gates.

Related literature: the comparison to ChenHuang2025, RudolphVanderLaan2017, Ma2023, and SmuclerLanniMasip2025 is useful but still high-level; add one sentence per closest paper specifying the estimand/inference object there and the precise dimension added here: transported ratio, weak denominator, expected-length frontier, or sample-learned cell weights.

Writing/register: the main text repeatedly lists long assumption checklists inside theorem prose, which makes the paper read like a formal artifact; keep the theorem statements precise but move repeated checklist commentary into compact named condition blocks or a table, preserving the exact \cref{} targets.

The abstract and introduction assert that the frontier is "characterized" and that the score-inversion set "attains this order," but the two-sided matching is proved with different constants on the two sides (c_0 = 3(1-alpha)^2/16 versus C_0 = max{2, 4L_alpha + 8/epsilon^2}, with L_alpha = sqrt(8/(alpha*epsilon^2))), and the ratio C_0/c_0 blows up as alpha -> 0 or epsilon -> 0. The abstract phrase "up to constants depending on the sampling ratio, overlap, and noncoverage level" appears only in the fixed-geometry sentence. Fix: in the abstract and in the paragraph after \cref{obj:thm:oracle-score-inversion-attainment} ("Combining \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse,obj:thm:oracle-score-inversion-attainment}, the oracle minimax expected length is characterized, up to constants, by ..."), state the explicit constant gap and its dependence on (alpha, epsilon), e.g. "the upper and lower constants differ by a factor of order (alpha*epsilon^2)^{-1/2}, so the characterization is a rate statement at fixed (alpha, epsilon)."

The abstract sentence "The unit-transport-weight least-favorable slice is embedded in the transported class, so its weak-ratio lower bound applies to the larger transported model" understates what the proof of \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} actually does: Steps 2-6 build the lower bound entirely on the geometry w = 1, e = 1/2, P_T = P_S^X, i.e. the no-covariate-shift case where kappa_n = 1. So the converse never exhibits a least-favorable configuration in which weight dispersion itself is the binding difficulty; the effective strength t_0 is achieved purely by shrinking mu_n. This matters because the paper's headline is that first-stage weakness and transport dispersion "enter through a common scale." Fix: add a remark after \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} stating plainly that the lower bound is witnessed at kappa_n = 1 and that the common-scale claim is established as an upper-bound phenomenon (via \cref{obj:thm:oracle-score-inversion-attainment}, whose radius scales with kappa_n-hat) plus a fixed-geometry statement uniform in g (\cref{obj:thm:fixed-geometry-frontier}), rather than by a dispersion-driven converse; alternatively, weaken the introduction sentence "The rate therefore treats a weak transported first stage and high transport dispersion symmetrically through n*mu_n^2/kappa_n."

\Cref{obj:ass:receipt-transport} (receipt-contrast transport) is imposed only as an equality of target-law averages, while \cref{obj:ass:outcome-transport} is conditional in x. The text flags the asymmetry ("The outcome condition is conditional in X, whereas the receipt condition is imposed at the target average") but never says why the weaker integrated form suffices or what it costs. In particular, the integrated condition is not implied by, and does not imply, cellwise transportability of compliance, and it is exactly the condition an applied reader would find hardest to defend since it is untestable from the source experiment alone. Fix: expand the paragraph following \cref{obj:ass:receipt-transport} into a short discussion giving (i) a primitive sufficient condition (e.g. conditional receipt transport in x, which is standard in \citet{ChenHuang2025}), (ii) an example where the integrated version holds but the conditional version fails, and (iii) a sentence on why the integrated form is the exact denominator link needed by \cref{obj:prop:compact-causal-range}.

The three envelope/dispersion/rate conditions (\cref{obj:ass:weight-envelope,obj:ass:weight-second-moment,obj:ass:degrading-array}) are each annotated only as "specific to this analysis," with no discussion of restrictiveness. Two substantive issues go unaddressed: (a) kappa_n <= k_n together with 0 <= w <= 2k_n is a strong coupling — it rules out weights that are bounded by 2k_n but concentrated, and the reader is not told which covariate-shift regimes (e.g. Gaussian location shift, logistic selection models) satisfy k_n = o(sqrt(n)); (b) \cref{obj:ass:degrading-array} forces k_n -> infinity and mu_n -> 0, so the model class deliberately excludes the fixed-strength and no-shift-with-bounded-weights regimes, yet the paper repeatedly speaks of "the transported class" as if it were the general model. Fix: add a paragraph after \cref{obj:ass:degrading-array} giving one worked covariate-shift example with explicit k_n and kappa_n, and stating which practically relevant arrays the degrading-array condition excludes and why the exclusion is harmless for a frontier statement.

The positioning paragraphs claim novelty relative to \citet{Ma2023}, \citet{SmuclerLanniMasip2025}, \citet{ChoiGuShen2018}, \citet{ChoiShen2019}, and \citet{ChenHuang2025} without any concrete comparison of what those papers prove. The sentences are of the form "The present paper adds target-covariate transport and an honest frontier indexed by n*mu_n^2/kappa_n" — the reader cannot tell whether the existing weak-IV LATE results already deliver an expected-length bound that would specialize to the w = 1 case in \cref{obj:prop:no-shift-reduction}, which is the natural benchmark. Fix: in the "Weak-IV and two-sample IV inference" paragraph, state for at least \citet{Ma2023} and \citet{AndrewsStockSun2019} what criterion they bound (coverage, length, power) and under what strength index, then say explicitly whether \cref{obj:prop:no-shift-reduction} recovers, sharpens, or is incomparable to their conclusion. Also add a citation for the Kish design-effect terminology, which is used throughout as "Kish-type dispersion" with no reference.

The appendix verification note leaves the formal scope ambiguous in a way that matters for how much weight a reader should put on the "checked" table. Two items: (i) \cref{obj:def:geometry-handle} is stated as a definition but its content is a pair of inequalities (chi-square bounded by exp(8*t_0*h^2), TV bounded by 2*rho) — these are lemmas, and the table lists no declaration for them, so it is unclear whether the Le Cam bounds are machine-checked or are unverified prose supporting \cref{obj:thm:fixed-geometry-frontier}; (ii) the proofs invoke an unnamed "generic affine-inversion length bound" and an "inflated affine-inversion length bound with Y = 8*B_{epsilon,c}" (in the proofs of \cref{obj:thm:fixed-geometry-frontier} and \cref{obj:thm:regular-cell-unknown-weight-attainment}) that is never stated anywhere in the paper. Fix: promote the two separation bounds out of \cref{obj:def:geometry-handle} into a stated lemma with its own row in the declaration table (or say in the note that they are verified inside fixed_geometry_frontier), and add an explicit display of the affine-inversion length bound in the appendix before its first use.

Introduction, paragraph 3: the phrase "The oracle benchmark allows procedures to use the transport weight w and the source propensity e" is accurate, but the surrounding summary sometimes reads as if the oracle result is the paper's operational recommendation; add one sentence distinguishing the oracle frontier from the later finite-cell feasible constructions and naming the exact extra finite-cell inputs needed for feasibility.

Setup, assumptions block: several assumptions are described as "standard" even when the paper uses a specialized integrated receipt-transport condition and degrading triangular-array restrictions; revise the prose after `ass:receipt-transport`, `ass:weight-envelope`, and `ass:degrading-array` to separate standard transport/IV content from paper-specific strength and growth restrictions.

Oracle Frontier section, theorem discussion: the sentence "This Anderson--Rubin style inversion is honest over P_n" in the abstract and main text should explicitly carry the stated overlap, envelope, second-moment, sample-size, and degrading-array conditions, because the formal theorem requires them.

Fixed Geometry section: the least-favorable construction is introduced as intuitive, but the paper gives little economic interpretation of the condition `p_n(x)` proportional to `w(x)`; add a short explanation that this concentrates complier mass according to target-weighted source regions and is a least-favorable calibration rather than a substantive compliance model.

Related Literature: the comparison to Chen-Huang, Rudolph-van der Laan, and weak-IV papers is useful but too compressed; add one or two precise contrasts about estimand, nuisance learning regime, and risk criterion so the contribution is positioned as an expected-length frontier rather than another identification or estimation result.

Appendix verification note: the manuscript repeatedly says proof narratives are expository companions to checked declarations, but it does not specify what parts are presentation-synthesized versus formally checked until the table; move a concise verification-scope sentence before the first theorem or at the start of the appendix to prevent readers from overreading checked status.

Abstract overstates the scope of the lower bound relative to what is proved. The abstract says the frontier is characterized 'over transported triangular arrays satisfying the stated overlap, sample-size, envelope, second-moment, and degrading-array conditions,' and the introduction says '\Cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} proves that every oracle honest confidence-set sequence over \(\mathcal P_n\) has limiting worst-case expected length at least a constant times \(\min\{1,t_0^{-1/2}\}\).' But the proof of \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} (Steps 2-6) constructs a single unit-weight, uniform-cell, \(e\equiv1/2\) geometry and derives the bound by embedding, so the converse constant is witnessed only by a \(\kappa_n=1\) slice in which no covariate shift occurs. The abstract sentence 'The unit-transport-weight least-favorable slice is embedded in the transported class, so its weak-ratio lower bound applies to the larger transported model' is accurate but is buried and does not govern the earlier sentences. Fix: in the introduction paragraph on \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse}, state explicitly that the converse is obtained by embedding the \(w\equiv1\) slice, so the lower bound demonstrates that dispersion cannot be exploited to beat \(\min\{1,t_0^{-1/2}\}\) rather than that dispersion itself drives the converse; and add one sentence noting that \cref{obj:thm:fixed-geometry-frontier} is what supplies a genuinely dispersed-geometry lower bound (with \(p_n(x)\propto w(x)\) in \cref{obj:def:least-favorable-witness}).

The 'uniform over all decompositions of the effective strength' clause is asserted repeatedly but never given operational content. It appears in the statement of \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} ('The same constants \(c_0\) and \(t_c\) apply uniformly over all decompositions of the effective strength \(t_0\) into the transported first-stage mean \(\mu_n\) and the weight dispersion \(\kappa_n\)'), in the following discussion paragraph, and in Step 10 of its proof, where the justification is only that 'the argument uses a row only through the threshold condition \(t_n=n\mu_n^2/\kappa_n\ge t_0\).' Since the witness geometry has \(\kappa_n\equiv1\), the clause as proved says the constants do not depend on how \(t_0\) is written, not that every \((\mu_n,\kappa_n)\) pair with \(n\mu_n^2/\kappa_n=t_0\) is separately attained by a witness. Fix: replace the clause with a precise statement — e.g. that \(c_0,t_c\) depend on \((c,\varepsilon,\alpha)\) only, and are in particular free of \(\mu_n\) and \(\kappa_n\) beyond their ratio — and delete the sentence in the discussion after \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} that reads it as an attainment claim over decompositions.

\cref{obj:ass:receipt-transport} is the paper's least standard assumption and receives the least scrutiny. It is imposed only at the target average — 'The target-population average of the conditional treatment-receipt contrast agrees across the two population states' — while \cref{obj:ass:outcome-transport} is conditional in \(x\). The text flags the asymmetry once ('The outcome condition is conditional in \(X\), whereas the receipt condition is imposed at the target average; this distinction is the transport structure used by the identification result below') and then cites \citet{ChenHuang2025} as if it were standard. An integrated condition is strictly weaker than its conditional counterpart but is also not implied by any primitive design feature, and it is the sole link making \(\mu_n\) the target complier share in \cref{obj:prop:compact-causal-range}. Fix: add a paragraph after \cref{obj:ass:receipt-transport} giving (i) a concrete design under which the integrated equality plausibly holds while the conditional one fails, (ii) an explicit note that the target complier share is identified only through this averaged equality, and (iii) a statement of what changes in \cref{obj:prop:compact-causal-range} if it fails — since a violation biases \(\mu_n\), the denominator, and hence has an amplified effect precisely in the weak regime the paper studies.

The envelope, second-moment, and degrading-array conditions are labelled 'specific to this analysis' but never assessed for restrictiveness or checked against a real design. \cref{obj:ass:weight-envelope} imposes \(w\le 2k_n\), \cref{obj:ass:weight-second-moment} imposes \(\kappa_n\le k_n\), and \cref{obj:ass:degrading-array} imposes \(k_n\to\infty\) with \(k_n=o(\sqrt n)\) and \(\mu_n\to0\). The accompanying remarks only restate them ('the sequence \(k_n\) controls the largest admissible density-ratio values while permitting the amount of covariate shift to grow with \(n\)'). Three questions go unanswered: whether \(\kappa_n\le k_n\) is implied by the envelope plus \(\mathbb E_S[w]=1\) or is a genuine extra restriction; why \(k_n\to\infty\) is required rather than permitted, since it excludes the bounded-shift case that most applications would satisfy; and what \(k_n=o(\sqrt n)\) rules out in terms of interpretable overlap between \(P_T\) and \(P_S^X\). Fix: add a short remark after \cref{obj:ass:degrading-array} answering these, ideally translating \(k_n=o(\sqrt n)\) into a statement about how badly the target may be allowed to concentrate on low-source-density covariate regions, and noting where in the proofs (the \(\delta_n=16k_n^2/n\) term in the coverage steps of \cref{obj:thm:fixed-geometry-frontier} and \cref{obj:thm:oracle-score-inversion-attainment}) the rate is actually used.

The 'Related Literature and Discussion' section states differences from the closest work without substantiating the comparison. On \citet{ChenHuang2025} — the paper whose assumption set is cited after nearly every assumption in \cref{sec:deferred-proofs}'s preceding section — the text says only that 'The present paper adds the honest minimax expected-length frontier for a compact transported-CACE ratio under a triangular-array weak first stage and Kish weight dispersion.' It is never stated whether the present model class \(\mathcal P_n\) is the same as, weaker than, or stronger than theirs, which matters because every standard-condition citation in the setup points there. Similarly, \citet{SmuclerLanniMasip2025} 'studies the properties of LATE confidence sets obtained by score-test inversion' — apparently the single-population analogue of \cref{obj:def:inversion-handle} — with no statement of whether their length results imply the \(w\equiv1\) case of \cref{obj:prop:no-shift-reduction}. Fix: add one sentence for each of these two papers stating the assumption-set relation explicitly, and, for \cref{obj:prop:no-shift-reduction}, say whether the reduction recovers a known single-population frontier or is new even at \(w\equiv1\).

The \(\mathcal N_n\) definition is presented twice in incompatible forms, and the appendix's account of the redundancy is unconvincing. The displayed inline definition '\(\mathcal N_n=\{P\in\mathcal P_n:P\text{ satisfies }\cref{obj:ass:finite-cell-source}\}\)' is followed by \cref{obj:def:finite-cell-class}, which re-lists all fifteen \(\mathcal P_n\) conditions plus \cref{obj:ass:finite-cell-source} while also requiring \(P\in\mathcal P_n\) — so the enumerated conditions are literally redundant given the membership requirement. The justifying sentence ('The anchored definition below is the verification checklist form of the same nesting, included so later theorem statements can point to the inherited restrictions explicitly') asks the reader to accept a formalization artifact as exposition. The same pattern recurs in \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse}, whose 'Transported-IV class' bullet re-lists all fifteen assumptions as a hypothesis even though they are definitionally true of any \(P\in\mathcal P_n\). Fix: keep the one-line inline definition of \(\mathcal N_n\) as the reader-facing statement, reduce \cref{obj:def:finite-cell-class} to '\(P\in\mathcal P_n\) and \cref{obj:ass:finite-cell-source}', and in \cref{obj:thm:oracle-converse} replace the two class bullets with 'the classes \(\mathcal P_n\) and \(\mathcal N_n\) are as in \cref{obj:def:model-class,obj:def:finite-cell-class}'.

Two prose claims in the appendix overview and \cref{obj:thm:oracle-score-inversion-attainment} are weaker or vaguer than the surrounding formal statements warrant. First, the closing sentence of \cref{obj:thm:oracle-score-inversion-attainment} — 'Consequently the oracle value in \cref{obj:def:oracle-value} satisfies the same attainable frontier order over fixed positive effective-strength thresholds' — is imprecise where the proof (Step 7) actually delivers the two-sided sandwich \(\tfrac{3(1-\alpha)^2}{16}\min\{1,t_0^{-1/2}\}\le V^\star(t_0)\le C_0\min\{1,t_0^{-1/2}\}\). Second, \cref{obj:prop:compact-causal-range}'s hypothesis 'The assignment outcome contrast and the receipt contrast for the source population satisfy the usual measurability and integrability conditions under the source covariate marginal \(P_S^X\)' is stated as an appeal to convention, whereas the proof's Steps 1, 3, and 4 use specific integrability facts derived from overlap and boundedness. Fix: replace the closing sentence of \cref{obj:thm:oracle-score-inversion-attainment} with the explicit two-sided display; and replace the 'usual conditions' hypothesis in \cref{obj:prop:compact-causal-range} with the actual requirement — measurable versions \(\Delta_Y,\Delta_D\) of the conditional contrasts existing and \(P_S^X\)-integrable — so the reader can check it.

Introduction, oracle frontier paragraph: the phrase “oracle procedures that know the transport weight and source propensity have minimax expected length” should state that the order is over the transported triangular-array class satisfying the listed overlap, envelope, second-moment, sample-size, and degrading-array conditions; add those conditions in the sentence to match the theorem scope.

Setup section, assumption commentary: several assumptions are described as “standard” while the paper uses a tailored transported-IV combination, especially receipt transport only at the target average; add a short paragraph explaining the empirical meaning and strength of outcome-contrast transport, receipt-contrast transport, and target complier positivity.

Fixed geometry section: the least-favorable construction is introduced before giving enough intuition for why complier probability proportional to the transport weight is economically or statistically natural; add a sentence tying this calibration to maximizing ratio uncertainty at fixed Kish dispersion.

Appendix proof narratives: the prose sometimes states formal-verification status and proof conclusions in ways that may read as stronger than the checked declaration list; keep the verification note separate from econometric proof intuition and state exactly which theorem declarations are checked.
